Because the season 2 actually ended with Homelander's realization that absolutely no one loves him, there is nobody on his side and the whole time everyone close despises him or using him for malevolent intentions. And that hurt his feeling and broke him like nothing else. So that (not killing him) is exactly what Butcher wanted from the beginning. Another part is how Butcher has changed and finally put away his indiscriminate hatred against all supes as he finally accepts Kimiko, Annie and Ryan. That also felt like a conclusion to this whole story. Still, optimistically waiting for season 3.

I thought the image of Frederick Vought as this moral-paragon, self-starter guy was a carefully engineered PR stunt. Does it not affect Vought's bottom line at all for Frederick to be revealed as a Nazi in those 1930's pictures with Stormfront? I thought it was weird for that not to come up at the press conference at the end, or anything. I'm iffy on Stormfront as a character, even now. I get the metaphor behind her and Homelander's relationship (the Nazi seducing and emboldening the right-wing American), but it comes off as kinda cowardly for the big bad to be a literal aspiring-Holocauster in a show all about critiquing American culture. Homelander, the conservative stars-and-stripes poster boy who exploits patriotism to justify corruption and evil, is a more "realistic" modern Nazi to me than the straight-up Nazi Party insider. The supe fights in the show (especially in this finale) are hard to enjoy because I still don't have a sense of what damage hurts supes and what they're basically immune to. Do punches and kicks actually do anything? Is "weaken them with blunt force and try to strangle/neck-snap them" the only way a hero can kill another hero of similar "power"? Why do supes hold off on using their OP moves (like Homelander's laser eyes, or the explodey-lightning Stormfront blew up that housing block with)? Funnily enough, this is the same thing that makes Marvel movies boring as hell to me. It's interesting how we've never seen a hero-versus-villain fight that could be described as such in-universe (we've really just seen "hero versus hero" fights). The few times we see them, like Homelander lasering that jihadi supe or that African supe, it's very one-sided. This fits the real-life terrorism metaphor really well: the idea that terrorists, like super villains, are a mostly-invented threat to justify defense spending and promote fealty to the state. This episode leaves me wondering about Neuman's goals. Is she a Vought insider or is she sincerely working to take Vought down? Why would it help her to kill all those people at the House committee hearing? It didn't seem like anyone who was going to testify had any dirt on her. If she is Vought, I don't see why she'd stay loyal to the company: Homelander sticks to Vought because he loves the feeling of power and prestige, but Neuman's already a congresswoman with her own base and isn't publicly involved with Vought anyway. Why not go completely rogue?

The political and social symbolism is great. Stormfront essentially shows how comfortable it is for right wing conservative megalomaniacs to align themselves with literal nazis (Homelander having a small wtf moment when SF started talking about white genocide was a great little detail). Stormfront being 100 years old and popping out of nowhere with memes and a different name is about the resurgence of of right wing nationalism with fancy branding and social media campaigns, and how easily the same themes from nazi Germany emerge again in the political discourse. And Vought portraying the danger of corporations getting too powerful and flying so high above the law is a bit ironic considering the platform the show is on, but as Los Pollos Hermanos man said - business always comes first, so I doubt Amazon care that much. I'm not too sure where they are going with fake AOC exploding heads randomly but I don't think there's a deep political message in this. Ffs at least I hope so, I really like AOC... And there's so much more - the celebrity church, the digs at MCU, the many issues with corporate "wokeism", toxic masculinity for lack of a better word (all the Boys dealing with their relationships in their distinct but also so familiar ways, and growing in the process - especially Frenchie's arc this season was so touching), actually well-written women dealing with (un)professional obstacles etc etc etc. The show is just too good. It's hype af, it's hilarious, it's dramatic, but there's also so many relevant topics and for me at least, none of them feel shoehorned or badly presented. I can write paragraphs about any one of these things. The last show that blew me away with this much competent writing, especially when building parallels to the world we are living in, was probably Mr. Robot. Just absolutely fantastic.

Since this thread is about S2 as a whole, I guess I'll post my thoughts here. I'll also probably get a lot of downvotes for this but.... I thought this season was more or less a repeat of S1 without the ability to be binged, both of which made this season enjoyable but not spectacular or addictive to me. S1 pushed so many boundaries just because it turned the superhero genre on its head and drizzled on a lot of adult material. S2 was the same, but because it was too much of the same, it came off as dull to me- nothing new, nothing groundbreaking, nothing exciting. It also didn't help that episodes came out once a week. With S1, while there were a lot of forgettable moments, if there was at least one super exciting thing in the last 10 minutes of the show, I could at least use that excitement to watch the next episode and continue to be immersed in my own excitement to elevate the next episode. With the weekly showing of this season, there may have been something exciting at the end, but that excitement is quickly forgotten and disappears by the time the next episode comes out. Take last week to this week for example- S2x07's cliffhanger was fantastic, but when this week's episode came out, I went into the episode thinking, "Okay, let's find out who the head exploder is" rather than "ZOMG I can't wait to find out who the head exploder is!!!!!!" Last thought, pacing felt atrocious, probably because of my previous two complaints (repetitiveness and weekly episodes). Based on what I know about S3, I feel like S2 and 3 should've been combined so that we can explore Vought's origins AND turn a few of The Seven into allies a lot quicker. Maeve, A-Train, and MAYBE Deep's betrayal of Vought should've come at ep 5,6,7 rather than 8 in my opinion- we all knew it was coming (at least I did).... and that anticipation should've paid off sooner than later where it felt like it was dragged out. Same thing with Vought's origins. What did we learn about Vought this season? We learned that its founder was Frederick, a Nazi, and Supes had been around since the 60s and gained popularity since.... that's it? Overall S2 seemed to be a telling of the consequences from S1's finale and a transition to S3 rather than a season in its own rights.

Ok I gotta say it.  Kripke's Supernatural formulas are showing through on this show. Supernatural formulas Kripke is following: Core good guys have plot armor.  Core good guys will not face any real risk until final season.  Only "good guys" that will die will be on periphery or bads converted to goods that deserve comeuppance/die for salvation. A main over-arching villain that also has plot armor until the final season.  To make up for this, a new mini-villain is introduced at the beginning of each season to be neutralized or killed by the end of each season. Because the "good guys" have plot armor, the only way to cause drama among them is to have them fight among themselves early/middle season then re-unite by end of season to take on that season's mini-villain. This isn't Kripke's, just something he follows, but nobody is dead until we see them dead.  Stormfront isn't dead.  She's just Satan.  Satan gets to come back a bunch of times. The real ultimate villain is "God".  The similarities here are obvious. So for me, going forward the show is a bit downgraded.  I don't really expect any of the core good guys to die except for 2 reasons, 1 we've reached the final season or 2, contractually they got a better offer to work on another show and their character needed to be killed off. I'll still watch, I watched every season of "The boys" which is what we called Supernatural before "The Boys" came out on TV, but it's now in the category of tchotchke TV for me like Supernatural, silly and fun, not at all serious, no real tension since we know the core goods and the main bad are being saved for the finale.

Finale was an absolutely fantastic episode and a testament to how true serialized story-telling via TV series can trump even Marvel's big hollywood budget films. The show still isn't immaculate enough that it doesn't have a tell for things it's trying to (e.g. it being obvious the Collective guy was going to die because they lingered on the shot for too long or that something was going to happen to Becca in the car because why else would they explicitly show a shot of it driving off like that, etc.), but that moment The Boys switched to The Girls was aces. I do have some mixed feelings about it refreshing the slate/format back to the beginning with Starlight being back on the Seven, the Boys having their records cleaned, and whatnot.
